recipes.title: Waterfalls
recipes.subtitle: Create smooth, flowing water
recipes.summary: Use a slow shutter speed to blur moving water while keeping the surrounding landscape sharp.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Adjust for the speed of the water and the amount of blur you want.

requirements.title: 16–35 mm
requirements.detail: A wide to standard-wide focal length works well for environmental compositions.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for reliably sharp surroundings at the recommended slow shutter speeds.

requirements.title: ND Filter
requirements.detail: Useful in daylight when the scene is too bright for a long exposure.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Optional for reducing reflections on wet rocks and foliage.

tips.title: Start Around 1 Second
tips.text: Begin around 1 second and adjust until the water has the amount of texture or smoothness you want.

tips.title: Watch the Highlights
tips.text: White water can overexpose easily, so check that bright areas retain detail.

tips.title: Protect the Lens
tips.text: Mist and spray can quickly cover the front element, so check and wipe it between compositions.

recipes.title: Sunrise & Sunset
recipes.subtitle: Capture color and dynamic light
recipes.summary: Sunrise and sunset combine dramatic color with rapidly changing light. Prioritize highlight detail and adjust your exposure as conditions change.

settings.label: Exposure Compensation
settings.note: Use negative compensation when the brightest parts of the sky are clipping.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Wide focal lengths show the environment; longer focal lengths isolate layers and the sun.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Optional, but useful as light levels fall.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Optional for controlling reflections. Use carefully on wide skies because polarization can become uneven.

tips.title: Arrive Early
tips.text: Set up before the best light arrives so you have time to find a strong composition.

tips.title: Stay Longer
tips.text: Some of the richest color can appear before sunrise or after sunset.

tips.title: Bracket Difficult Light
tips.text: When the sky is much brighter than the foreground, capture a short exposure bracket so you have more options later.

recipes.title: Forest
recipes.subtitle: Photograph detail in complex scenes
recipes.summary: Forest scenes can be visually busy and often contain large differences between light and shadow. Look for simple compositions, layers and directional light.

requirements.title: 24–100 mm
requirements.detail: Wide views capture the environment while short telephoto focal lengths help isolate details.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Useful for reducing reflections on leaves and wet foliage.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Optional in dim woodland when shutter speeds become too slow to handhold.

tips.title: Simplify the Scene
tips.text: Use paths, individual trees, light or repeating patterns to create structure.

tips.title: Check the Edges
tips.text: Small branches and bright gaps near the frame edge can easily distract from the subject.

tips.title: Use Soft Light
tips.text: Overcast conditions often reduce harsh highlights and make woodland color and detail easier to control.

recipes.title: Mountains
recipes.subtitle: Capture scale and layered landscapes
recipes.summary: Mountain photography is about scale, depth and light. Use foreground elements and atmospheric layers to give large landscapes a sense of dimension.

requirements.title: 16–200 mm
requirements.detail: Wide lenses emphasize scale; telephoto lenses isolate and compress mountain layers.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Useful for reducing reflections and increasing contrast in suitable light; the effect depends strongly on the sun angle.

tips.title: Create Depth
tips.text: Include foreground, middle ground and distant peaks when the scene allows it.

tips.title: Try a Telephoto
tips.text: Longer focal lengths can isolate mountain layers and make distant peaks feel visually closer.

tips.title: Watch the Weather
tips.text: Clouds, haze and rapidly changing light can transform mountain layers, so keep reassessing the scene.

recipes.title: Long Exposure
recipes.subtitle: Turn movement into smooth textures
recipes.summary: Long exposures record movement over time, allowing you to smooth water, stretch clouds or create light trails while stationary elements remain sharp.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Longer exposures create more pronounced movement.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: A versatile range for landscapes, architecture and moving water.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Strongly recommended for exposures lasting several seconds.

requirements.title: ND Filter
requirements.detail: Often needed for multi-second exposures in daylight.

tips.title: Use a Timer
tips.text: A short self-timer can prevent movement caused by pressing the shutter button.

tips.title: Experiment
tips.text: Compare several shutter speeds rather than assuming the longest exposure will look best.

tips.title: Check for Movement
tips.text: Inspect the frame for wind-blown foliage, people or other elements that may blur in a distracting way.

recipes.title: Outdoor Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Create natural portraits outdoors
recipes.summary: Outdoor portraits combine subject placement, background control and natural light. Use a wider aperture and suitable camera position to separate your subject from the environment.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: Normal to short-telephoto focal lengths are versatile for individual portraits.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: A wider maximum aperture makes background separation easier.

tips.title: Focus on the Eyes
tips.text: Use eye detection when available, or place the focus point on the nearest eye.

tips.title: Check the Background
tips.text: Move slightly if distracting objects intersect with the subject.

tips.title: Keep Shutter Speed Up
tips.text: Even with a wide aperture, make sure shutter speed stays high enough to avoid subject movement.

recipes.title: Golden Hour Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Use warm, soft evening light
recipes.summary: Golden hour provides warm, directional light that can flatter skin tones and create atmospheric backgrounds.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: A versatile range for portraits with flattering working distance.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: Useful for subject separation as the light level falls.

tips.title: Try Backlighting
tips.text: Placing the sun behind the subject can create a warm rim light around hair and clothing.

tips.title: Watch for Flare
tips.text: Lens flare can be creative, but reposition slightly if it reduces contrast too much.

tips.title: Expose for Skin
tips.text: Check the subject's face rather than judging exposure only from the bright sky behind them.

recipes.title: Indoor Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Make the most of available light
recipes.summary: Indoor portraits often require balancing limited light with enough shutter speed to keep your subject sharp.

requirements.title: 35–85 mm
requirements.detail: Useful for portraits when working space is limited.

requirements.title: F2.8 or faster
requirements.detail: Helps gather light indoors and isolate the subject.

tips.title: Find Window Light
tips.text: Position the subject near a window for a large, soft and directional light source.

tips.title: Accept Higher ISO
tips.text: A sharp portrait with some noise is often preferable to a blurred image at lower ISO.

tips.title: Mind Mixed Lighting
tips.text: Different indoor light sources can create conflicting color casts, so simplify the lighting when possible.

recipes.title: Group Photo
recipes.subtitle: Keep multiple people sharp
recipes.summary: Group photos require more depth of field than individual portraits. Keep people on a similar focus plane and avoid using an aperture that is too wide.

requirements.title: 28–70 mm
requirements.detail: Moderate wide to normal focal lengths are practical for groups without extreme edge distortion.

tips.title: Keep People Aligned
tips.text: Arrange people at roughly the same distance from the camera when possible.

tips.title: Take Several Frames
tips.text: Multiple frames reduce the chance of someone blinking or looking away.

tips.title: Focus Into the Group
tips.text: For deeper rows, focus slightly behind the front row rather than on the person nearest the camera.

recipes.title: Stars
recipes.subtitle: Capture a clear star-filled sky
recipes.summary: Photographing stars requires gathering plenty of light while keeping the shutter speed short enough to prevent obvious star trails.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Shorten the exposure if stars begin to appear stretched.

requirements.title: 14–24 mm
requirements.detail: Wide focal lengths make it easier to include more sky and use longer exposures before trails become obvious.

requirements.title: F2.8 or faster
requirements.detail: A fast lens helps collect more light during a short exposure.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for stable multi-second exposures.

tips.title: Focus Carefully
tips.text: Use magnified live view on a bright star and adjust focus until it appears as small and sharp as possible.

tips.title: Find Dark Skies
tips.text: Moving away from strong artificial lighting can reveal significantly more stars.

tips.title: Turn Off Stabilization on a Tripod
tips.text: When the camera is firmly mounted, disable stabilization if your camera or lens recommends doing so.

recipes.title: Milky Way
recipes.subtitle: Reveal detail in the night sky
recipes.summary: Milky Way photography combines a dark location, a fast lens and careful exposure to reveal structure that is difficult to see with the naked eye.

requirements.title: 14–24 mm
requirements.detail: A wide focal length captures more of the sky and foreground.

requirements.title: F2.8 or faster
requirements.detail: A fast maximum aperture helps collect more starlight.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for stable multi-second exposures.

tips.title: Plan the Composition
tips.text: The Milky Way changes position through the night and year, so planning helps place it where you want.

tips.title: Shoot RAW
tips.text: RAW files preserve more flexibility for adjusting shadows, white balance and noise.

tips.title: Check the Histogram
tips.text: A dark-looking preview can be misleading at night, so use the histogram to confirm that important tones are recorded.

recipes.title: Blue Hour
recipes.subtitle: Capture the transition into night
recipes.summary: Blue hour occurs around twilight when the sky takes on a deep blue tone while enough ambient light remains to balance naturally with artificial lighting.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: A practical tripod-based range; handheld shooting requires a faster shutter speed and usually a higher ISO.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Versatile for cityscapes, architecture and landscapes.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Recommended as ambient light fades, especially when you want low ISO and deeper depth of field.

tips.title: Be Ready Early
tips.text: The best balance between sky brightness and artificial lighting can last only a short time.

tips.title: Try Reflections
tips.text: Water and wet surfaces can reflect blue-hour color and city lights.

tips.title: Keep Shooting
tips.text: Light levels and color balance change quickly, so capture several variations as the sky darkens.

recipes.title: City at Night
recipes.subtitle: Capture lights, streets and architecture
recipes.summary: Night cities combine bright artificial lights with deep shadows. Stabilize the camera when possible and expose carefully to preserve illuminated details.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Use this range when the camera is supported. Handheld shooting requires a faster shutter speed and usually a higher ISO.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Useful for wide cityscapes through tighter architectural details.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Recommended for lower ISO, smaller apertures and longer exposures; handheld shooting is also possible with faster shutter speeds.

tips.title: Protect Bright Lights
tips.text: Avoid overexposing important signs, windows and streetlights where you want detail.

tips.title: Use Movement Creatively
tips.text: Longer shutter speeds can turn moving cars into light trails while buildings remain sharp.

tips.title: Use a Hood
tips.text: A lens hood can help reduce flare from streetlights and other bright sources just outside the frame.

recipes.title: Pets
recipes.subtitle: Capture sharp, expressive moments
recipes.summary: Pets can move unpredictably, so use continuous autofocus and a fast shutter speed while paying close attention to the eyes and expression.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: Flexible for close portraits and action at moderate distances.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: Useful for indoor light and background separation.

tips.title: Get Low
tips.text: Photographing near the animal's eye level often creates a more engaging perspective.

tips.title: Use Short Bursts
tips.text: Short bursts improve your chance of capturing the best expression or moment.

tips.title: Use a Familiar Sound
tips.text: A quiet sound or cue can briefly direct the animal's attention toward the camera without forcing the pose.

recipes.title: Wildlife
recipes.subtitle: React quickly to unpredictable subjects
recipes.summary: Wildlife photography requires fast reactions, reliable autofocus and enough shutter speed to deal with unpredictable movement.

requirements.title: 200–600 mm
requirements.detail: Telephoto reach helps photograph distant wildlife without approaching too closely.

requirements.title: Stabilization
requirements.detail: Helpful when handholding long focal lengths, especially for relatively still subjects.

tips.title: Prioritize Shutter Speed
tips.text: Use enough shutter speed for the subject rather than trying to keep ISO unnecessarily low.

tips.title: Leave Room to Move
tips.text: Avoid framing too tightly when an animal may suddenly change direction.

tips.title: Respect Distance
tips.text: Use focal length rather than moving too close, especially when an animal changes behavior because of your presence.

recipes.title: Birds in Flight
recipes.subtitle: Freeze fast movement in the air
recipes.summary: Birds in flight demand fast shutter speeds, continuous autofocus and enough space in the frame to follow unpredictable movement.

requirements.title: 300–600 mm
requirements.detail: Long telephoto reach is useful for small and distant birds.

requirements.title: Stabilization
requirements.detail: Can help steady the viewfinder and reduce camera movement while tracking.

tips.title: Start Around 1/2000 s
tips.text: This is a practical starting point for freezing much of the wing and body movement.

tips.title: Leave Space Ahead
tips.text: Give the bird room in the frame in the direction it is flying.

tips.title: Track Before the Burst
tips.text: Acquire and follow the bird before pressing the shutter so autofocus has time to settle on the subject.

recipes.title: Sports
recipes.subtitle: Freeze decisive action
recipes.summary: Sports photography is about anticipating action and keeping moving subjects sharp. A fast shutter speed and continuous autofocus are the priorities.

requirements.title: 70–300 mm
requirements.detail: A useful range for many field and court sports, depending on working distance.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: A moderately fast lens helps maintain action-stopping shutter speeds and subject separation.

tips.title: Anticipate the Action
tips.text: Watch the activity and prepare for moments before they happen rather than reacting afterward.

tips.title: Use Short Bursts
tips.text: Shoot around peak moments rather than holding the shutter continuously for long periods.

tips.title: Choose a Clean Background
tips.text: When possible, position yourself so the action is separated from spectators, signs and other distractions.

recipes.title: Panning
recipes.subtitle: Show speed with motion blur
recipes.summary: Panning uses a slower shutter speed while following a moving subject, keeping the subject relatively sharp while turning the background into directional blur.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Start around 1/60 s and adjust for subject speed.

requirements.title: 35–200 mm
requirements.detail: Choose focal length based on subject distance and how tightly you want to frame it.

requirements.title: Panning Stabilization
requirements.detail: If your lens or camera has a panning-specific stabilization mode, it can be useful.

requirements.title: ND Filter
requirements.detail: Optional in bright daylight when you cannot reach a slow enough shutter speed at the lowest ISO.

tips.title: Follow Before Shooting
tips.text: Start tracking smoothly before pressing the shutter.

tips.title: Follow Through
tips.text: Continue the panning motion after the exposure instead of stopping abruptly.

tips.title: Practice at One Speed
tips.text: Repeat the same subject speed and shutter speed for several passes before making larger adjustments.

recipes.title: Lakes & Reflections
recipes.subtitle: Use calm water as part of the composition
recipes.summary: Still water can mirror skies, mountains and trees. Balance exposure carefully and decide whether you want to preserve or reduce reflections.

settings.label: Exposure Compensation
settings.note: Use slight negative compensation if bright sky reflections are clipping.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Wide to normal focal lengths work well for symmetrical scenes and environmental context.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Recommended when light is low or when you want precise framing.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Optional. A polarizer can reduce glare, but it can also weaken the reflection you are trying to photograph.

tips.title: Look for Calm Conditions
tips.text: Early mornings and sheltered water often produce cleaner reflections.

tips.title: Try Symmetry
tips.text: Place the shoreline near the center when the reflection is a major part of the image.

tips.title: Rotate the CPL Slowly
tips.text: Watch the reflection while rotating the polarizer and stop before the effect becomes too strong.

recipes.title: Seascapes
recipes.subtitle: Shape waves, coastlines and moving water
recipes.summary: Seascapes combine moving water with strong horizons and foreground detail. Shutter speed determines whether waves look crisp, textured or smooth.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Shorter exposures retain wave texture; longer exposures create smoother movement.

requirements.title: 16–50 mm
requirements.detail: Wide focal lengths help include foreground rocks, coastline and sky.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for consistent sharpness at the recommended slow shutter speeds.

requirements.title: ND Filter
requirements.detail: Useful in daylight when you want slower shutter speeds.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Optional for controlling glare on rocks and shallow water.

tips.title: Time the Waves
tips.text: Release the shutter as water moves through the composition rather than shooting randomly.

tips.title: Keep the Horizon Level
tips.text: Small horizon errors are especially obvious in open seascapes.

tips.title: Protect Your Gear
tips.text: Salt spray can build up quickly, so clean the front element and avoid changing lenses in heavy spray.

recipes.title: Rivers & Streams
recipes.subtitle: Use flowing water to lead through the frame
recipes.summary: Rivers and streams can become strong leading elements. Use shutter speed to control texture while keeping surrounding details sharp.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Adjust to preserve some texture in the moving water.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Wide to normal focal lengths cover both environmental views and tighter stream details.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for consistent sharpness at the recommended slow shutter speeds.

requirements.title: ND Filter
requirements.detail: Useful when ambient light is too bright for the shutter speed you want.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Useful for reducing glare on wet rocks and seeing through shallow water.

tips.title: Use the Water as a Leading Line
tips.text: Position bends and channels so they guide the eye into the scene.

tips.title: Keep Some Texture
tips.text: Extremely long exposures can remove all character from smaller streams.

tips.title: Watch Wet Highlights
tips.text: Reflective rocks and white water can clip before the rest of the scene.

recipes.title: Fog & Mist
recipes.subtitle: Create simple, atmospheric landscapes
recipes.summary: Fog reduces contrast, hides distant detail and simplifies complex scenes. Use that separation to build layered, minimal compositions.

settings.label: Exposure Compensation
settings.note: Bright fog can cause the meter to render the scene darker than expected.

requirements.title: 24–200 mm
requirements.detail: Normal and telephoto focal lengths are especially useful for isolating layers in fog.

tips.title: Look for Layers
tips.text: Trees, hills or buildings at different distances become naturally separated by haze.

tips.title: Expose the Fog Brightly
tips.text: Check the histogram and avoid letting white fog become dull gray unless that is intentional.

tips.title: Simplify Aggressively
tips.text: Fog is most effective when the frame contains only a few strong shapes.

recipes.title: Snow Landscapes
recipes.subtitle: Keep bright snow clean and detailed
recipes.summary: Snow can fool camera meters into underexposing the scene. Add exposure when needed while preserving texture in the brightest areas.

settings.label: Exposure Compensation
settings.note: Adjust while watching highlights; the exact amount depends on how much snow fills the frame.

requirements.title: 16–200 mm
requirements.detail: Wide lenses show the environment while telephoto lenses isolate snowy details and layers.

requirements.title: CPL Filter
requirements.detail: Optional for reducing glare and deepening contrast in suitable light.

tips.title: Watch the Histogram
tips.text: Aim for bright snow without pushing important highlights off the right edge.

tips.title: Protect Batteries
tips.text: Cold temperatures can reduce battery performance, so keep a spare warm when possible.

tips.title: Check White Balance
tips.text: Snow can pick up strong blue casts in shade; decide whether to keep or neutralize them.

recipes.title: Environmental Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Show the person and the place together
recipes.summary: Environmental portraits use surroundings to add context. Keep enough depth of field for the location to remain recognizable without letting it overpower the subject.

requirements.title: 24–70 mm
requirements.detail: Wide-normal focal lengths include context while keeping perspective manageable when you avoid placing faces near the frame edges.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: A moderately fast lens gives flexibility between context and separation.

tips.title: Let the Background Explain Something
tips.text: Include details that add information about the subject rather than random clutter.

tips.title: Avoid Edge Distortion
tips.text: Keep faces away from the extreme edges when using wider focal lengths.

tips.title: Balance Subject and Scene
tips.text: Move yourself before reaching for a wider aperture; composition should do most of the work.

recipes.title: Backlit Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Control bright light behind your subject
recipes.summary: Backlighting can create rim light and atmosphere, but the subject's face can become too dark. Meter carefully and add fill light when needed.

settings.label: Exposure Compensation
settings.note: Increase exposure when the face is too dark, while checking bright background highlights.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: Normal to short telephoto focal lengths work well for subject separation.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: A wider aperture helps isolate the subject and soften a bright background.

requirements.title: Flash
requirements.detail: Optional fill flash can lift the face when the background is much brighter than the subject.

tips.title: Shade the Lens
tips.text: Use a hood or your hand outside the frame to reduce unwanted flare.

tips.title: Expose for the Face
tips.text: Evaluate skin tones separately from the brightness of the background.

tips.title: Use the Rim Light
tips.text: Position the subject so the backlight outlines hair or shoulders instead of disappearing directly behind them.

recipes.title: Couples
recipes.subtitle: Keep two people connected and sharp
recipes.summary: Couple portraits need enough depth of field for both faces while still separating them from the background. Pose them close to the same focus plane when possible.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: Normal to short telephoto focal lengths give comfortable working distance and flattering perspective.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: Useful for separation while keeping both people sharp.

tips.title: Keep Faces on a Similar Plane
tips.text: Depth of field is easier to manage when both subjects are similar distances from the camera.

tips.title: Create Interaction
tips.text: Small actions and eye contact often look more natural than two people simply facing the camera.

tips.title: Check Both Faces
tips.text: Zoom in after a few frames to confirm that both sets of eyes are sharp.

recipes.title: Children
recipes.subtitle: React quickly to natural movement
recipes.summary: Children rarely stay still for long. Prioritize shutter speed and continuous autofocus, then let moments happen rather than over-directing them.

requirements.title: 35–135 mm
requirements.detail: A flexible range lets you work nearby or give the subject more space.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: Helpful for maintaining faster shutter speeds in lower light.

tips.title: Stay Ready
tips.text: Keep the camera awake and settings prepared because good moments often happen between posed frames.

tips.title: Use Short Bursts
tips.text: A few frames around peak movement usually work better than long uncontrolled bursts.

tips.title: Photograph at Their Level
tips.text: Lower camera positions often create more direct and engaging images.

recipes.title: Street Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Work quickly in real-world surroundings
recipes.summary: Street portraits combine people with uncontrolled backgrounds and changing light. Use a compact setup and settings that let you react quickly.

requirements.title: 35–85 mm
requirements.detail: Normal focal lengths balance context, working distance and subject separation.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: Useful when moving between shade, indoor spaces and evening light.

tips.title: Choose the Background First
tips.text: Find clean light or a strong backdrop, then place the subject within it.

tips.title: Keep the Setup Simple
tips.text: Avoid changing too many settings when the light and subject can change quickly.

tips.title: Respect the Subject
tips.text: For directed portraits, communicate clearly and work efficiently once someone agrees to be photographed.

recipes.title: Moon
recipes.subtitle: Reveal detail on the lunar surface
recipes.summary: The moon is much brighter than the night sky. Use a telephoto lens, low ISO and a relatively fast shutter speed to preserve surface detail.

requirements.title: 200–600 mm
requirements.detail: Long focal lengths make the moon large enough in the frame to show surface detail.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Optional but useful for precise framing at very long focal lengths.

tips.title: Do Not Expose for the Sky
tips.text: The surrounding sky can be almost black while the moon itself remains correctly exposed.

tips.title: Use Magnified View
tips.text: Check critical focus on the moon's edge or surface features.

tips.title: Try Different Phases
tips.text: Side lighting around quarter phases reveals more crater relief than a flat full moon.

recipes.title: Light Trails
recipes.subtitle: Turn moving lights into lines of motion
recipes.summary: Long exposures can transform moving vehicle lights into continuous trails while buildings and streets remain sharp.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Adjust for traffic speed and how far you want the trails to travel through the frame.

requirements.title: 16–70 mm
requirements.detail: Wide to normal focal lengths work for roads, intersections and city context.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for sharp stationary elements during multi-second exposures.

tips.title: Build the Composition First
tips.text: Treat roads and buildings as the composition; the light trails should support it.

tips.title: Wait for Enough Traffic
tips.text: A longer exposure is not useful if too few lights pass through the frame.

tips.title: Protect Highlights
tips.text: Bright headlights and signs can clip quickly, so check the brightest parts of the image.

recipes.title: Star Trails
recipes.subtitle: Record the apparent movement of the night sky
recipes.summary: Star trails show Earth's rotation by combining long total exposure time with a fixed composition. Stacking multiple shorter frames is often more flexible than one extremely long exposure.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Capture many frames and stack them for longer trails.

requirements.title: 14–35 mm
requirements.detail: Wide focal lengths make it easier to include both sky movement and foreground context.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: A fast lens helps record more stars in each exposure.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required so every frame aligns precisely.

tips.title: Keep Everything Consistent
tips.text: Do not move the tripod or change focus once the sequence begins.

tips.title: Use an Interval Timer
tips.text: Small gaps between frames can create breaks in stacked trails.

tips.title: Plan the Direction
tips.text: The look of the trails changes depending on where the camera points in the sky.

recipes.title: Night Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Balance a person with low ambient light
recipes.summary: Night portraits need enough shutter speed for the subject while preserving some ambient light. A fast lens and optional flash make the balance easier.

requirements.title: 35–85 mm
requirements.detail: Normal focal lengths work well in tight nighttime environments.

requirements.title: F2.8 or faster
requirements.detail: A fast lens helps keep ISO and shutter speed under control.

requirements.title: Flash
requirements.detail: Recommended when you need consistent light on the subject while preserving ambient light in the background.

tips.title: Expose the Background First
tips.text: Set ambient exposure to the level you want, then add light to the subject if needed.

tips.title: Use Available Light
tips.text: Shop windows, signs and streetlights can become useful directional light sources.

tips.title: Check Face Sharpness
tips.text: Low light can reduce autofocus reliability, so inspect the eyes after important frames.

recipes.title: Fireworks
recipes.subtitle: Capture bright bursts and light trails
recipes.summary: Fireworks are bright but brief. Use a tripod and multi-second exposures to record complete bursts while keeping the surrounding scene sharp.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: Open the shutter as a burst begins and shorten the exposure if multiple bursts overlap too heavily.

requirements.title: 24–100 mm
requirements.detail: Choose focal length based on your distance and whether you want to include the environment.

requirements.title: Tripod
requirements.detail: Required for sharp multi-second exposures.

tips.title: Frame Wider Than You Think
tips.text: Firework bursts can spread beyond the area where they first appear.

tips.title: Avoid Overlapping Too Many Bursts
tips.text: Too many explosions in one exposure can create a bright, cluttered frame.

tips.title: Set Focus Before the Show
tips.text: Once focus is established on a distant object, switch to manual so it does not hunt in the dark.

recipes.title: Wildlife Portrait
recipes.subtitle: Isolate a relatively still animal
recipes.summary: Wildlife portraits emphasize expression, eye contact and background separation. Use enough shutter speed for small movements while letting the lens isolate the subject.

requirements.title: 200–600 mm
requirements.detail: Telephoto reach lets you isolate animals without approaching too closely.

requirements.title: Stabilization
requirements.detail: Helpful for steady framing when handholding long focal lengths.

tips.title: Focus on the Eye
tips.text: The nearest visible eye is usually the most important sharp detail.

tips.title: Watch the Background
tips.text: Small changes in your position can remove branches or bright patches behind the animal.

tips.title: Wait for Expression
tips.text: Ears, head angle and eye direction can change the feeling of the portrait.

recipes.title: Birds Perched
recipes.subtitle: Capture detail in relatively still birds
recipes.summary: Perched birds allow more careful composition than birds in flight. Prioritize eye sharpness, clean backgrounds and enough shutter speed for subtle movement.

requirements.title: 200–600 mm
requirements.detail: Long focal lengths help fill the frame without disturbing the bird.

requirements.title: Stabilization
requirements.detail: Helpful when handholding and framing small subjects at long focal lengths.

tips.title: Keep the Eye Sharp
tips.text: Even a mostly still bird can move its head suddenly, so maintain active autofocus.

tips.title: Use the Perch
tips.text: Branches, reeds and posts can become part of the composition rather than just a place for the bird to sit.

tips.title: Leave Looking Room
tips.text: Give the bird extra space in the direction it is facing.

recipes.title: Running Pets
recipes.subtitle: Freeze fast movement close to you
recipes.summary: Running pets require faster shutter speeds than relaxed portraits. Continuous autofocus, short bursts and enough framing space improve your chances of a sharp peak-action image.

requirements.title: 50–200 mm
requirements.detail: A short telephoto range gives useful working distance while keeping the pet large in the frame.

requirements.title: F5.6 or faster
requirements.detail: Useful for maintaining action-stopping shutter speeds.

tips.title: Pre-Focus the Action Area
tips.text: If the pet runs through a predictable zone, begin tracking before it reaches the best position.

tips.title: Leave Framing Space
tips.text: Fast subjects are easier to keep in frame when you do not compose too tightly.

tips.title: Shoot at Peak Motion
tips.text: Look for moments when paws leave the ground or the body reaches a strong, readable position.

recipes.title: Indoor Sports
recipes.subtitle: Freeze action in difficult indoor light
recipes.summary: Indoor sports combine fast movement with limited light. Prioritize shutter speed, use a fast lens and accept higher ISO rather than allowing motion blur.

settings.label: ISO
settings.note: High ISO values are normal indoors; prioritize the shutter speed needed to stop action.

requirements.title: 50–200 mm
requirements.detail: Useful for courts, halls and closer indoor action.

requirements.title: F4 or faster
requirements.detail: A fast lens is especially valuable under dim venue lighting.

tips.title: Accept High ISO
tips.text: Noise is easier to manage than motion blur from a shutter speed that is too slow.

tips.title: Watch Light Flicker
tips.text: Some artificial lights vary through the power cycle and can cause inconsistent exposure or color.

tips.title: Anticipate Peak Action
tips.text: Prefocus your attention on likely moments such as jumps, shots, tackles or reactions.

recipes.title: Motorsport
recipes.subtitle: Freeze speed or emphasize motion
recipes.summary: Motorsport can be photographed with very fast shutter speeds for frozen detail or slower panning speeds for a stronger sense of motion.

settings.label: Shutter Speed
settings.note: For panning, experiment around 1/60–1/250 s instead.

requirements.title: 70–300 mm
requirements.detail: Telephoto focal lengths are useful when working from spectator areas or trackside positions.

requirements.title: Stabilization
requirements.detail: A panning mode can help when deliberately using slower shutter speeds.

tips.title: Choose Freeze or Motion
tips.text: Decide whether the image should show sharp mechanical detail or a blurred sense of speed.

tips.title: Track Before Shooting
tips.text: Follow the vehicle smoothly before starting a burst.

tips.title: Use Safe Positions
tips.text: Photograph only from designated areas and never trade safety for a better angle.
